body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Party banter for one act: nine short exchanges between companions, spoken as the party walks about the Hollow. There are no Narrator rows, no options and no replies in banter. Every row is a companion talking to another companion, never to the player.

HOW BANTER WORKS. While the party explores, now and then one exchange plays as a few lines of chat between two or three companions who happen to be in the party, once each, on entering an area. The area is unknown: write chat that could happen anywhere on a walk (the weather, the night, food, rest, habits, each other's quirks, the Express, the moon, the road, old trades and old manners). Only two or three of the six are ever in the party, so each exchange stands alone, mentions nobody else, and needs no setup. Banter is funny first; one line in an exchange may turn honest, never more.

ACT ONE. The party has only just met: the Ghostlight Express crashed hours ago, and these six are strangers thrown together in the Hollow. Wary, curious, sizing each other up, first impressions and first friction, small kindnesses by accident. Nobody knows anyone's past. The hound is only ever called Dreadfang.

BANTER RULES.
1. Each exchange is 4 to 6 SAY rows, each a companion's single line (one or two short sentences, under about 28 words), alternating naturally between the speakers; a trio may let the third speak last or interrupt. Every speaker in the list speaks at least once.
2. Use only the facts in the attached voice sheets and fact lists, plus the pairing seeds. Never state or hint at any companion's past or secret, and never say what anyone's debt is. No new named people, places or monsters beyond those named. No two exchanges may share a joke or a topic; no line may repeat a line in a voice sheet.
3. Pet phrases: each at most once in the whole reply. Companions call each other by first name unless their voice sheet says otherwise.
4. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks). No em dashes, semicolons, brackets, asterisks or stage directions. No game terms. Our own words.

THE NINE EXCHANGES (in this order; the topic of each is yours, chosen from the seeds and facts):
EXCHANGE 1: Rook + Tobin (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, tobin_hayward)
EXCHANGE 2: Rook + Silas (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, silas_vane)
EXCHANGE 3: Tobin + Delphine (speaker ids: tobin_hayward, delphine_ravelle)
EXCHANGE 4: Silas + Lucan (speaker ids: silas_vane, lucan_houndstooth)
EXCHANGE 5: Lucan + Cordelia (speaker ids: lucan_houndstooth, cordelia_skein)
EXCHANGE 6: Rook + Lucan (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, lucan_houndstooth)
EXCHANGE 7: Silas + Delphine (speaker ids: silas_vane, delphine_ravelle)
EXCHANGE 8: Rook + Tobin + Lucan (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, tobin_hayward, lucan_houndstooth)
EXCHANGE 9: Silas + Delphine + Cordelia (speaker ids: silas_vane, delphine_ravelle, cordelia_skein)

PAIRING SEEDS (optional starting points, from the characters' files; use a seed at most once, and a pair listed twice must not reuse one):
- Rook and Tobin: Rook plants his shield between Tobin and a smouldering ember; Tobin asks why a grave-guard cares about straw and twine; Rook says a watchman counts everyone on the parish roll, in bone or burlap.
- Rook and Silas: a procedural watchman and a card sharp: tallies and ledgers, shift logs and fine print.
- Tobin and Delphine: two sewn folk: Tobin fusses over her frayed cuffs and she over his seams; Your Foolishness has opinions about straw.
- Silas and Lucan: a gambler and a hunter: odds against grades out of ten; the hound and the shadow; Lucan corrects Silas's grammar.
- Lucan and Cordelia: a hunter who grades monsters and a scientist who catalogues specimens: they argue about whose notes are better, and the hound gets examined.
- Rook and Lucan: the ghost hound sits on Rook's armoured boot and yips; Rook deadpans that an unlicensed phantom mastiff breaks three municipal leash statutes; Lucan insists the hound has sensed a doom-laden draught.
- Silas and Delphine: thick as thieves: a three-card monte and a shared contempt for the house; they compare the fine print on their leashes.
- Tobin and Lucan: Lucan sniffs Tobin's straw and woodsmoke and scores the bouquet nine out of ten for rustic comfort; the hound never chews Tobin's hem.
- Silas and Cordelia: a skeleton who reads a room by his rattle meets a woman who reads a room by pulses; ribs and viscosity.
- Delphine and Cordelia: tailoring and seams: Delphine eyes Cordelia's eight-sleeved waistcoat; Cordelia admires Delphine's stitching; two women who made themselves something other than what they were made as. Light and funny only.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line:

EXCHANGE <number>
SAY <speaker id>: <line>
SAY <speaker id>: <line>
...

Use the speaker ids exactly as given (for example SAY rook_coldwake: ...). Write exactly nine EXCHANGE blocks, numbered 1 to 9, and nothing else.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write: `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/banter-cast-1.md` (the voice sheets and fact lists for Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward and Silas Vane) and `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/banter-cast-2.md` (the same for Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein).
result:
EXCHANGE 1
SAY rook_coldwake: Mind the turf, Tobin, there is a live cinder blowing off that wreckage. I will plant the coffin-lid here until the wind settles.
SAY tobin_hayward: Why does a northern grave-guard care if a bundle of dry straw and burlap catches a stray spark? You have no skin in this row.
SAY rook_coldwake: A watchman counts every soul on the parish roll, whether he walks in bone or burlap. Unlawful combustion on a public verge is still my docket.
SAY tobin_hayward: Fair enough, keep that heavy plank between me and the ash. One hot coal in my lapel and the mice will never forgive either of us.

EXCHANGE 2
SAY silas_vane: That is a soggy old ledger you are nursing, friend, and here I thought I was the only man keeping score in this valley.
SAY rook_coldwake: Shift log and headstone rubbings, properly indexed by parish and drainage grade. What sort of book are you keeping inside your coat?
SAY silas_vane: Just a few chalk tallies inside my ribs for favours owed and tabs left open. Keeps the arithmetic close to the chest where nobody can smudge it.
SAY rook_coldwake: Chalk on bare bone will rub off in the damp before the week is out. If you want an audit to stand, you need proper wax and slate.
SAY silas_vane: Tell's in the twitch, friend, and the day I let an auditor look under my shirt is the day I fold for good.

EXCHANGE 3
SAY tobin_hayward: Hold still, you're fraying at the left wrist and that running stitch is far too loose for wet weather. Who cobbled your hem together?
SAY delphine_ravelle: I do my own needlework, darling, and a stage cuff is cut on the bias for dramatic flair, not for digging turnips in a ditch.
SAY tobin_hayward: Dramatic flair will not keep the damp out of your stuffing when the rot sets in. Tell that floating head on your shoulder to stop grinning at my straw.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Your Foolishness says a gentleman stuffed with prime hay should not lecture a headliner on tailoring. Keep your shears to yourself before I unpick that burlap collar.

EXCHANGE 4
SAY silas_vane: Ten to one the next thing that jumps us out of the brush has more teeth than manners, friend. Care to lay a modest stake on the card?
SAY lucan_houndstooth: A gentleman does not wager on the noble art of the field, Silas, he grades the specimen out of ten by posture and spoor. And it is "fewer manners", if you please.
SAY silas_vane: You can grade my grammar when that phantom mutt of yours stops eyeing my shadow like a spare soup bone.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Dreadfang, Harbinger of the Pale Shroud, merely notes that your shadow lags half a pace behind your boots. In Edwardia, we deduct two points for tardy footwork.
SAY silas_vane: Look at the coat on him, friend, that hound would bolt at a clap of thunder if the house didn't hold his leash.

EXCHANGE 5
SAY cordelia_skein: Fascinating pathology on your spectral companion, Lucan, though I cannot quite chart how an ectoplasmic thorax sustains that volume of yipping. May I take a tiny sample?
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Good heavens, madam, you will keep your needles away from Dreadfang, if you please. He is a harbinger of dread omen, not a frog on a lecture slab.
SAY cordelia_skein: And yet your leather journal grades road-beasts like prize marrows at a county fair. My crimson silk notes record exact humours and ratios before dissolving cleanly into mist.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: A proper field naturalist preserves his observations in permanent ink for posterity, Cordelia. Hush now, the dark has teeth, and your six eyes are clicking loud enough to wake the brush.

EXCHANGE 6
SAY rook_coldwake: Your phantom hound is sitting squarely on my left greave, Lucan, and it just yipped twice. An unlicensed mastiff on a public footpath breaks three municipal leash statutes.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Step lightly, Rook, for when Dreadfang gives voice upon cold iron, he has scented a doom-laden draught rising from the Hollow. It is a most solemn omen.
SAY rook_coldwake: He is sniffing my rations bag where I wrapped a crust of salt cheese in waxed paper. Even the brass knocker on my shield stayed quiet for that.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Aged dairy carries a spectral resonance very similar to ancient barrow-rot, if you please. Come along, good boy, leave the watchman's boots to their municipal duty.

EXCHANGE 7
SAY silas_vane: Watch the queen of bones, darling, three cards on the knee and not a single mark on the backs. Pick the lady and I let you keep that shiny new button.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Please, I grew up in Picco where the barkers palm aces in their sleep, and you flashed the corner on the second shuffle. House always wins, unless you rigged the shoe yourself.
SAY silas_vane: Sharp eyes, even if one of them is oversized glass. Your floating friend over there is rattling his non-existent jaw like he wants in on the cut.
SAY delphine_ravelle: He says you're lying, and he doesn't even have eyes, though he respects a hustler who reads the fine print before signing his name.
SAY silas_vane: Nobody reads the fine print in time, darling, we just keep shuffling until the dealer looks away.

EXCHANGE 8
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Forgive the liberty, Tobin, yet the bouquet of dry meadow-straw and aged turnip around your shoulders earns a generous nine out of ten for rustic comfort. It reminds one of an autumn harvest.
SAY tobin_hayward: It is fifty-year rot and damp soil you are smelling, Lucan, and you can stop sniffing my collar like a lost hound. Rook, tell him to take a pace back.
SAY rook_coldwake: The ground here has poor subsidence and the mist carries every cellar damp in the district. You ought to remind me to take a breath before I judge the air myself.
SAY tobin_hayward: Take your breath now, Rook, and let it out slow so you do not rattle. At least the wolf-man's ghost dog has the sense not to chew my hem.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Dreadfang respects a well-tended seam, friends, though I maintain the vintage has a pleasingly crisp finish.

EXCHANGE 9
SAY delphine_ravelle: Eight sleeves in charcoal silk and every single armhole set on the true bias, Cordelia. Whatever tailor stitched that waistcoat deserves top billing on the marquee.
SAY cordelia_skein: Thank you, darling, it is a joy to meet someone who appreciates proper anatomical calibration in a garment. Your own patchwork shows remarkably resilient tension across the thorax.
SAY silas_vane: Wonderful, I am walking through a haunted valley with a pair of haberdashers while the chill in my ribs says the road ahead is rigged.
SAY cordelia_skein: Your ribs are whistling in a brisk minor key, Silas, which suggests high atmospheric moisture rather than imminent ambush. Do hold still, this will only tingle if I check your joints.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Leave the poor skeleton his rattle, darling, it is the only percussion our little troupe has left.
